posts.text:
Welcome to Nyaya on Telegram.

From 1 July 2024, the BNS, BNSS and BSA replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act. Every section number you learnt changed. This channel helps you relearn them, a few minutes a day.

What you get here:
• 9 am, Mon–Sat: one IPC section and where it lives in the BNS now (#OldToNew)
• 7:30 pm, daily: a quiz poll with the answer explained (#Quiz)
• Sunday: one landmark judgment, briefed (#Landmark)
• Friday and Saturday: explainers and the week in the Supreme Court

Useful links:
Student tools (case briefs, moots, quizzes): https://asknyaya.in/students?utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel
IPC ↔ BNS converter: https://asknyaya.in/convert?utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel
News explained: https://asknyaya.in/explained?utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel

Nyaya is a free legal research site that answers from real Supreme Court and High Court judgments, with sources cited. Research help, not legal advice.

Forward this to your class group if it helps.

#OldToNew · IPC 302 → BNS 103(1)

Punishment for murder.
Old: IPC s.302
New: BNS s.103(1): death or imprisonment for life, and fine.

Exam trap: s.103 punishes murder; it doesn't define it. The definition (old IPC s.300) is now BNS s.101.

New in s.103: sub-section (2) covers murder by a group of five or more on grounds such as race, caste, community or personal belief. The IPC had nothing like it.

Check any section: https://asknyaya.in/convert?q=IPC+302&utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel

posts.question: From which date do the BNS, BNSS and BSA apply?
posts.explanation: In force from 1 July 2024. Offences and proceedings from before that date are still governed by the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act.

posts.text:
#OldToNew · IPC 420 → BNS 318(4)

Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property.
Old: IPC s.420
New: BNS s.318(4): up to 7 years, and fine.

Exam trap: the definition of cheating (old IPC s.415) is now BNS s.318(1). Simple cheating (old IPC s.417) is s.318(2). The whole cheating family now sits in one section.

https://asknyaya.in/convert?q=IPC+420&utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel

posts.question: IPC s.300 defined murder. Which BNS section defines it now?
posts.explanation: BNS s.101 defines murder and s.103 punishes it. s.100 is culpable homicide (old IPC s.299).

posts.text:
#OldToNew · IPC 498A → BNS 85

Cruelty by a husband or his relatives.
Old: IPC s.498A
New: BNS s.85: up to 3 years, and fine.

Exam trap: the meaning of "cruelty" (the old Explanation to s.498A) is now its own section, BNS s.86. Questions often ask for s.86, not s.85.

https://asknyaya.in/convert?q=IPC+498A&utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel

posts.question: Anticipatory bail (CrPC s.438) is now in:
posts.explanation: BNSS s.482. Bail in non-bailable offences (old CrPC s.437) is s.480; special powers of the High Court and Sessions Court (old s.439) are s.483.

posts.text:
#OldToNew · IPC 307 → BNS 109(1)

Attempt to murder.
Old: IPC s.307
New: BNS s.109(1): up to 10 years and fine; if hurt is caused, up to imprisonment for life.

Exam trap: the aggravated form (attempt by someone already serving a life sentence, with hurt caused) is s.109(2), punishable with death or imprisonment for life.

https://asknyaya.in/convert?q=IPC+307&utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel

posts.question: Which BNS section defines "cruelty" for the offence that replaced IPC s.498A?
posts.explanation: s.85 punishes cruelty by a husband or relatives; s.86 defines cruelty (the old Explanation to s.498A). s.80 is dowry death.

posts.text:
#OldToNew · IPC 379 → BNS 303(2)

Theft.
Old: IPC s.379
New: BNS s.303(2): up to 3 years, or fine, or both.

What's new: a repeat conviction for theft carries rigorous imprisonment of 1 to 5 years, and fine. For a first-time theft of property worth less than ₹5,000, where the property is returned or its value restored, the court can order community service.

The definition of theft (old IPC s.378) is s.303(1).

posts.question: The certificate for electronic records (Evidence Act s.65B) is now in:
posts.explanation: BSA s.63, with the certificate format in the Schedule. s.61 says an electronic record can't be refused merely for being electronic.

#OldToNew · IPC 34 → BNS 3(5)

Acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention.
Old: IPC s.34
New: BNS s.3(5)

Exam trap: it isn't a standalone section any more. It's sub-section (5) of s.3, "General explanations". In an FIR or chargesheet you'll now see "BNS 103(1) r/w 3(5)" where you used to see "IPC 302 r/w 34".

posts.question: For offences punishable with 3 to 7 years, BNSS s.173(3) allows a preliminary enquiry before an FIR. It must be completed within:
posts.explanation: 14 days, with prior permission from an officer not below the rank of DSP, to check whether there is a prima facie case.

posts.text:
#Landmark · Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)

Citation: (1973) 4 SCC 225 · decided 24 April 1973
Bench: 13 judges, the largest the Supreme Court has ever sat. Majority 7:6.

Facts: A Kerala math head challenged state land reform laws. The case grew into a question about the Constitution itself: how far can Parliament amend it under Article 368?

Issue: Is Parliament's amending power unlimited?

Held: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including fundamental rights, but it cannot destroy or damage its basic structure.

Why it matters:
• Partly overruled Golaknath (1967), which had said fundamental rights could not be amended at all.
• Created the basic structure doctrine. The judges gave examples (supremacy of the Constitution, democracy, secularism, separation of powers, federalism), not a closed list.
• Applied later in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) and Minerva Mills (1980).

Exam line: "Amend, yes; abrogate, no."

More case briefs and moot practice: https://asknyaya.in/students?utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel

posts.question: How many judges sat on the bench in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)?
posts.explanation: 13, the largest bench ever. By 7:6 it held Parliament can amend the Constitution but not its basic structure.

#OldToNew · IPC 120B → BNS 61(2)

Punishment of criminal conspiracy.
Old: IPC s.120B (and the definition in s.120A)
New: BNS s.61: the definition is s.61(1), the punishment s.61(2).

Two sections became one section with two sub-sections, a pattern you'll see across the BNS.

https://asknyaya.in/convert?q=IPC+120B&utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel

posts.question: Which of these IPC offences has NO counterpart in the BNS?
posts.explanation: The BNS has no counterpart to s.377. Stalking is BNS s.78, s.509 is s.79, rash driving is s.281.

posts.text:
#OldToNew · IPC 506 → BNS 351(2) and 351(3)

Criminal intimidation.
Old: IPC s.506 (definition in s.503)
New: BNS s.351. The definition is s.351(1). The punishment is s.351(2): up to 2 years, or fine, or both.

Exam trap: a threat to cause death or grievous hurt, to destroy property by fire, and similar serious threats fall under s.351(3): up to 7 years, or fine, or both.

https://asknyaya.in/convert?q=IPC+506&utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel

posts.question: Under BNSS s.187, police custody of up to 15 days in total can be authorised:
options: Only in the first 15 days after arrest
In whole or in parts, within the first 40 or 60 days of detention
Only after the chargesheet is filed
Never; only judicial custody is allowed
posts.explanation: The 15 days can be split and used within the first 40 or 60 days (of a 60- or 90-day total). Under CrPC s.167 it was read as the first 15 days only.

posts.text:
#OldToNew · IPC 304B → BNS 80

Dowry death.
Old: IPC s.304B
New: BNS s.80: at least 7 years, up to imprisonment for life.

Same ingredients: death of a woman by burns, bodily injury or in unnatural circumstances within 7 years of marriage, after cruelty or harassment linked to a dowry demand "soon before her death".

The presumption that goes with it (old Evidence Act s.113B) is now BSA s.118.

https://asknyaya.in/convert?q=IPC+304B&utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel

posts.question: Murder by a group of five or more on grounds such as race, caste, community, sex, language or personal belief is covered by:
posts.explanation: BNS s.103(2): each member is punishable with death or life imprisonment, and fine. The IPC had no such provision.

#OldToNew · IPC 354D → BNS 78

Stalking.
Old: IPC s.354D
New: BNS s.78. First conviction: up to 3 years, and fine. Subsequent conviction: up to 5 years, and fine.

Neighbours to remember: IPC 354 → BNS 74, IPC 509 → BNS 79.

posts.question: The rule that information from an accused in police custody leading to discovery of a fact can be proved (Evidence Act s.27) is now in:
posts.explanation: The proviso to BSA s.23(2). s.23 also carries over old ss.25–26: confessions to police, or in police custody, can't be proved.

#OldToNew · IPC 499/500 → BNS 356

Defamation.
Old: IPC s.499 (definition) and s.500 (punishment)
New: BNS s.356(1) defines it; s.356(2) punishes it with simple imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both, or community service.

What's new: community service is now one of the possible sentences. It's one of the new punishments added by BNS s.4(f).

posts.question: Snatching is now a separate offence under the BNS. Which section?
posts.explanation: BNS s.304: up to 3 years and fine. Under the IPC, snatching was charged as theft or robbery. s.303 is theft.

#OldToNew · IPC 124A → BNS 152

Sedition is gone, at least in name.
Old: IPC s.124A (sedition). Kept in abeyance by the Supreme Court in S.G. Vombatkere v. Union of India (2022).
New: BNS s.152, "Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India": imprisonment for life or up to 7 years, and fine.

Exam angle: the word "sedition" doesn't appear in the BNS. s.152 targets acts against India's sovereignty, unity and integrity rather than "disaffection towards the Government".

posts.question: How many sections does the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 have?
posts.explanation: The BNS has 358 sections (the IPC had 511). The BNSS has 531 and the BSA 170.

posts.text:
#Landmark · Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014)

Citation: (2014) 8 SCC 273 · decided 2 July 2014
Bench: Chandramauli Kr. Prasad and Pinaki Chandra Ghose, JJ.

Facts: A husband accused under IPC s.498A and the Dowry Prohibition Act sought anticipatory bail. The Court used the case to address routine arrests.

Issue: Can police arrest automatically for offences punishable with up to 7 years?

Held: No. For such offences, police must be satisfied that arrest is necessary on the grounds in CrPC s.41 and record their reasons. Magistrates must check those reasons before authorising detention.

The directions:
• Police to use a checklist of the s.41(1)(b)(ii) grounds and send it, with reasons, to the Magistrate.
• Where arrest isn't needed, serve a notice of appearance (CrPC s.41A) within 2 weeks of the case being registered.
• Police who don't comply face departmental action and contempt; Magistrates who authorise detention mechanically face departmental action.

Where it lives now: the arrest power and the notice of appearance are in BNSS s.35. The Court reaffirmed these directions in Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022).

More case briefs and moot practice: https://asknyaya.in/students?utm_source=telegram&utm_medium=channel

posts.question: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) told police not to arrest automatically for offences punishable with imprisonment of up to:
posts.explanation: 7 years. Police must record reasons for arrest; the notice of appearance (old CrPC s.41A) is now in BNSS s.35.
